## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada* ("Eating stored food", Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 38) proscribes the consumption of food that has been stored overnight [SuttaCentral; Vinayamukha II 1973]. According to the rule, a bhikkhu who accepts food, retains it overnight, and eats it the following day incurs a *pācittiya* offense [Vinayamukha II 1973]. The origin story and ruling are set at Sāvatthī, establishing an offense for consuming stored edibles (*sannidhikāraka*), though allowances were subsequently granted for monks undertaking arduous journeys [Vinayamukha II 1973; Vinayamukha III 1983]. Linguistically, the term *sannidhikārakam* functions as a rare quasi-gerund or adverbial gerund in *-akam* in the Pātimokkha, shared with Nissaggiya Pācittiya 23 and cited in canonical discussions of householder habits and storing provisions [Collins 1993; Collins 2005]. In historical Vinaya accounts of the Second Council at Vesālī, this rule is directly invoked in condemning *siṅgiloṇakappa* (the practice of storing salt in an animal horn for later use) as an illicit indulgence [Bapat 1956; Sarao and Long 2017; Vinayamukha III 1983].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral demonstrate that this prohibition was universally maintained across early Buddhist monastic traditions, with corresponding rules in the Prātimokṣa and Vibhaṅga texts of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, and Mahāsāṅghika recensions, as well as the Theravāda Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (Pācittiya 121) and its sectarian counterparts [SuttaCentral; Clarke 2009]. SuttaCentral also notes a thematic resemblance in the *Sattasatikakkhandhaka* (Cullavagga 22) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies substantial internal text reuse across 82 Pali texts, most heavily with adjacent dietary rules in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (Pc 37, Pc 35, Pc 36), the Katāpattivāra of the Parivāra (Pvr 1.2), and Pāṭidesanīya rules (Pd 1, Pd 3, Pd 4) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language matching, DharmaNexus aligns the text with Tibetan canonical Vinaya commentaries and treatises, including the *Pratimokṣasūtrapaddhati* (D4104), the *Bhikṣuṇīvinayavibhaṅga* (D0005), and the *Vinayasūtravṛtti* (D4122) [DharmaNexus].
